title: Stride
subtitle: Workout Tracking App - UX Case Study
overview: Stride is a mobile workout tracker that helps people build routines, start sessions fast, and stay consistent through a streak-based home screen. The product covers onboarding states, habit-forming feedback, and a scalable component system across the Home and Workouts tabs.
problem: Many fitness apps lose people in the first week. Setup feels heavy: before a beginner can do anything, they face a blank app and have to build a plan from scratch. Progress is also invisible: without quick feedback, there is little reason to come back tomorrow.
solution: A home screen that works as a launchpad. Quick start sits above the fold, empty states explain the next step, a weekly streak gives progress at a glance, and a routine library makes past sessions easy to repeat. Every screen is built from the same small set of components, so empty and active states feel like one product.

features.title: Home - empty state
features.description: A first-run home that replaces the blank screen with an encouraging hero card, a persistent Quick start action, and a flame counter that introduces the streak from the first launch.

features.title: Home - active state
features.description: A weekly streak tracker with completed, current and upcoming days, plus a this-week overview of sessions, time and energy, and recent workouts that can be repeated.

features.title: Workouts - empty state
features.description: A single illustration, one explanation and one primary action, so the only next step is to create a first routine.

features.title: Workouts - populated
features.description: A routine library of workout cards with a colour marker, type tag, exercise count, description, Start session button and overflow menu.

architecture.title: One small system, four different states
architecture.description: The interface is built from a small set of reusable parts, so all four screens feel like one product. Colour carries meaning, typography keeps hierarchy calm, and an 8pt grid keeps spacing predictable across empty and populated states.
highlights: Colour: deep purple for brand and action, light purple for tags, green for completed states and orange for the streak flame
Typography: one sans-serif family with a defined title, heading, body, caption and label scale
Spacing: an 8pt grid for margins, padding and gaps
Components: primary button, tag pill, workout card, stat tile, streak day circle and tab bar
Navigation: a three-tab bar with a clear purple active state

results.description: Two tabs, each shown empty and populated
Home and Workouts designed end to end
One clear call to action per empty state

problemPoints.description: Without quick feedback, there is little reason to come back tomorrow.

study.problemStatement: How might we help a first-time user start a workout within seconds, and give them a reason to return the next day?
goals: Reduce the time from opening the app to starting a session.
Make empty states feel like guidance, not dead ends.
Reinforce consistency with visible, lightweight progress.
Let people build and reuse their own routines.

research.intro: The first-run experience and the return loop were the two moments worth designing for. I compared three established products to see how they handle first launch, quick start and progress display before setting direction.

competitors.name: Nike Training Club
competitors.focus: Strong guided content and a confident first-run path. The catalogue is the product, so starting is easy but returning to a self-built routine is not the focus.

competitors.name: Strava
competitors.focus: Progress is cumulative and social. Streaks and weekly totals motivate, but the depth suits committed athletes more than first-week beginners.

competitors.name: Hevy
competitors.focus: Fast logging and a reusable routine library. The closest match to the problem: repeat a session without rebuilding it.

hypotheses: Beginners want to start now and organise later, so a persistent Quick start action matters.
A streak is a simple, proven motivator, but it must be readable at a glance.
Users returning daily want to repeat past workouts, not rebuild them.

persona.name: Irene
persona.summary: Wants to build a regular workout habit. She has tried apps before and quit because planning felt like homework.
needs: Start a session without building a plan first.
See a small sign of progress on the first screen.
Repeat a workout that already worked.

principles.title: Start fast
principles.description: The primary action is always one tap away.

principles.title: Guide, don't block
principles.description: Empty states point to the next step instead of stopping the user.

principles.title: Show progress early
principles.description: Small wins appear on the first screen, not buried in a history tab.

principles.title: Stay calm and focused
principles.description: One brand colour, generous spacing and few competing actions.

study.screensIntro: Four screens cover the two most important moments in the product: arriving for the first time, and returning once a habit starts to form. Each tab is designed in both its empty and populated state so the system holds together before any data exists.
study.screensNote: Each screen is shown with the decision that shaped it and the changes made between drafts, so the reasoning stays attached to the interface it produced.

screens.imageAlt: Stride home screen in its empty state with a purple hero card, Quick start workout button and a saved workouts hint
screens.lead: A first screen that points forward.
body: The first-time experience replaces the usual blank home with a hero card: an encouraging message and an illustration on the brand purple. Quick start workout sits directly beneath it as the primary action, while a flame counter in the top right begins at zero.
Below, Saved workouts explains where routines will live, so the space below the fold has a purpose from the first launch.
screens.decision: Quick start sits above the fold, so a new user can begin without creating anything first. Saved workouts below gives routines a home, so the space under the primary action still has a purpose.
iterations: Gave the first screen one job: start a workout. Quick start sits directly beneath the hero card.
Moved the saved workouts area below the primary action, so planning never delays the first session.
Introduced the streak counter at zero on first launch, with a tooltip that names the mechanic before it is earned.

screens.imageAlt: Stride home screen in its active state with a weekly streak tracker, weekly overview tiles and recent workouts
screens.lead: Progress you can read in one glance.
body: Once the user has trained, the hero card becomes a weekly streak tracker. Day circles show completed days with a green check, today highlighted, and the days still to come.
This week overview summarises sessions, total time and energy burned. Recent workouts sits below it, giving past routines a place to resurface without leaving the home screen.
screens.decision: Progress is shown as a week at a glance, not a long history. It keeps the screen light while still rewarding consistency.
iterations: Set the week to start on Sunday so the day labels and the streak logic agree.
Corrected the streak data so the current streak never exceeds the personal best.
Raised the contrast of inactive day circles against the purple card.
Increased caption text to a readable minimum size.

screens.imageAlt: Stride Workouts tab in its empty state with an illustration, explanatory copy and a Create my first workout button
body: The Workouts tab for a user with no routines: a single illustration, a short explanation and one primary button, Create my first workout.
screens.decision: One action only. Everything on this screen exists to push the user toward creating a routine.
iterations: Rebalanced the content vertically so the illustration and action sit together instead of floating in empty space.
Aligned the title position with Screen 4 so both Workouts states share a layout.

screens.imageAlt: Stride Workouts tab populated with four saved workout cards, tags, exercise counts, Start session buttons and an overflow menu
screens.lead: A routine library built for repeat sessions.
body: Each card carries a colour marker, workout name, type tag, exercise count, a short description, a Start session button and an overflow menu for edit and delete.
The card keeps starting a session in the foreground while edit and delete stay one level back, so the list stays quiet until someone needs it.
screens.decision: Starting a session is the card's main job, so the button is always visible rather than hidden behind a detail page.
iterations: Mapped the coloured left bar to category so it carries meaning instead of decoration.
Moved edit and delete behind the overflow menu, keeping the card focused on starting a session.
Set one card rhythm across the list: name and tag, then exercise count and description, then the action.

system.intro: The interface is built from a small set of reusable parts, so all four screens feel like one product. Colour carries meaning, type keeps the hierarchy calm, and the 8pt grid keeps spacing predictable between empty and populated states.

type.usage: Tags, tab labels and micro copy

system.spacing: An 8pt grid drives margins, padding and gaps. Screen padding is 24pt, card padding is 16 to 20pt, and vertical rhythm steps in multiples of 8.
system.navigation: A three-tab bar (Home, Workouts, Profile) with a purple active state and grey inactive icons. Home and Workouts are the designed scope; Profile is shown for completeness.
system.note: This page doubles as the style guide: the colour tokens, type scale, spacing rule and component list above are the same ones used across all four screens, so new screens can be assembled without redrawing the basics.

metrics.intro: These are the metrics used to judge whether the first-run flow and the streak loop are working.

items.label: Activation
items.description: Percentage of new users who complete a first workout in their first session.

items.label: Time to first workout
items.description: Seconds from first launch to starting a session.

items.label: Habit
items.description: Average streak length and the share of users who start a session from Recent workouts.

items.label: Creation
items.description: Percentage of users who save at least one custom routine in week one.

learnings: Empty states are a real design opportunity, not an afterthought.
Consistent content and data matter as much as visuals. Mismatched tags and impossible streak numbers weaken an otherwise strong screen.
Reducing the number of actions on a screen made the primary action clearer.
A small design system pays off twice: it speeds up empty and populated states, and it exposes inconsistencies early.
nextSteps: Design the core loop: in-workout screen, rest timer and session summary.
Build the workout creation flow behind the plus action.
Design the Profile tab and settings.
Run usability tests with five people and iterate on the first-run flow.
Add dark mode and accessibility checks for contrast, text size and touch targets.
